title: Broken cisterns (Jeremiah 2:13)
hookLine: they left the fountain of living waters for cisterns that hold no water

cards: In a dry land, rain doesn't fall all year. So people dug cisterns: pits cut into the rock to catch the rain and keep it for the dry months. A good cistern is a lifeline.

A cracked one is worse than none, because you only find out when you lower the bucket and it comes up empty. Now set a spring next to that, water rising out of the ground on its own, cold and moving, free for anyone.
Jeremiah puts the two side by side, in a single verse.

teach.b: "For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water."

Two evils, and they're a pair: leaving the spring, and then the digging. Hewing a cistern out of rock is hard labor. The people aren't lazy in this picture; they're exhausted, working hard on something that leaks.
Living water, in Hebrew mayim chayim, means water that moves, from a spring or a stream, not water that sits. In this verse, God is that spring.
The broken cisterns, in the chapter around it, are the other gods and the foreign powers the people chased, even going to Egypt and Assyria to drink their rivers' water.
Earlier, God asks whether any nation has ever changed its gods, and says my people have changed their glory for what doesn't profit. A cistern isn't bad in itself.

teach.h: A CISTERN THAT KEEPS EVERY DROP.
teach.b: The Mishnah, in Pirkei Avot, praises a great student, Rabbi Eliezer, as a plastered cistern that never loses a drop: someone who keeps everything he learns. The trouble isn't storing water.
It's trading a spring for a container, and then a container that cracks.
The rabbis also compared the words of Torah to water, reading Isaiah's call to everyone who is thirsty to come to the waters as an invitation to learn.
So the verse leaves a practical question: what am I working hard to fill that never stays full?

how: Jeremiah 2, with its broken cisterns, is read in synagogue as a haftarah in the summer weeks before Tisha b'Av, when the Prophets' words of warning are read.

jars smashed in mourning when a king died
pits dug with great effort that can't hold water

p: a cistern that keeps every drop

they hew out cisterns from rock: hard work on something that leaks.

games.q: there's a spring of living water close by, free and flowing. what do the people in Jeremiah's verse do?
o: drink from the spring every day.
dig their own cisterns, which crack.
wait for rain and do nothing.
games.why: they forsake the fountain and hew out broken cisterns that can hold no water: hard work, and an empty bucket.

practice: Look back over the last week and find one place your time and effort poured in and drained right out: an app you refresh, an argument you keep rehearsing, a purchase that was supposed to fix something.
No need to judge yourself; just see it clearly, the way you'd see a crack in a bucket. Then picture one living thing that could take its place: a walk, a call, a page of learning.

wordCard.voice: Broken cisterns. Pits dug with great effort that can hold no water, set beside the spring the people walked away from. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a spring, free for anyone. Nobody has to dig for it. That's day seven hundred ninety-nine.
